other three you could argue for, so that Obtenebration has its full

functionality. Eyes are strong Auspex, but are they that rare?

> four more Camarilla starters right away.  Maybe a conflict-themed
> expansion (a la KMW), with four clanless decks: Camarilla/Imperator,

understand why it was unavailable in the last major Cam reprint!

It's been in starters here and there but given its extreme utility a
reprint would be cool. Mythic Form, while expensive, is a strong card
for Protean that I would like to see reprinted. I wouldn't mind
seeing Tongue of the Serpent and Skin of the Adder reprinted for

Cheers,

Well, that is completely true. That being said, some unfun cards

unfun, the newer players say "Wow. This game blows. Why are those
incredibly powerful, incredibly unfun cards so hard to get and never
reprinted, so only old players get to use them..."

happy if I never saw it again. But that it exists, and that some
players already have it, and it isn't getting banned from play, it
should get reprinted at some point.

To take this argument in a different direction, not disagreeing with
LSJ, or really with Kevin...

I do agree that Sens Dep is anti-fun, but it's also my experience that
it doesn't make you win. Ravnos decks that concentrate on Sens Dep
seem to put a lot of effort into blood management and stealth, to the
point where there's not a whole lot of ousting mechanism. The prey of
a Sens Dep-heavy deck tends to wall up (to the degree that it can),
and Sens Dep-ing backwards seems like a good way to oust your predator
with little net result except a new pred with more pool. It's rare
that I've seen a Ravnos deck actually *win* when it plays Sens Dep
(more than just 1 or 2 as a prayer card). The Ravnos decks I've seen
do well are swarm bleed, with Week of Nightmares, Paul Forrest, Club
Illusion, or a combination thereof. I feel like an Eldest are Kholo
deck could be really good, though I haven't seen one win yet.
There's always some fun Mata Hari BS that might work sometimes...
Ravnos have some good intercept too, and I'm sure that somebody has a
good Smiling Jack/Constant Revolution-type wall deck. (Granted, a
decent amount of this is conjecture, as there's only one *good* Ravnos
deck in our playgroup that I've seen played a lot, which is Eric
Simon's Phaedymite deck with DEM/CHI. The only other player that I've
played a lot with who really liked Ravnos could never really get them
banging on all cylinders, and moved to LA a few years back and is now
in Phoenix.)

Now, maybe I'm wrong. Maybe there are more Ravnos decks out there
that I don't know about that win while playing a lot of Sens Dep...
But if I'm right, then reprinting a card that's anti-fun and doesn't
help you win doesn't seem like it helps out newbies much at all. If
anything, it just helps them build decks that are anti-fun *and*
losers, meaning that everyone at the table is miserable.

Granted, it's a powerful card that due to not being reprinted is way
rarer than it should be, and so I'm not *against* reprinting it. But
being powerful doesn't necessarily mean "makes you win"... And if it
doesn't make you win, then there's no disadvantage to not having it,
right?

While I don't necessarily agree with the degree of problem others feel
it causes and/or whether it should be reprinted, I do agree with this
- part of the reason it is viewed as an 'anti-fun card' is that having
the ability to remove it is frequently dependent on what deck you
played, unlike most other lock-down cards.

For instance, Pentex Subversion locks a vampire mostly down - but it
can be readily removed (or at least the attempt can be made) no matter
what cards you have in your library. Same holds true with any 'D to
remove' card, or even those that time out via counters - removing the
card isn't reliant on your own deck choices.

Sense Dep, however, pretty much requires your deck to be able to
remove a vampire from play, either by rushing him, or intercepting him
with combat behind it, or by playing a specialized card that flips him
back to uncontrolled, etc. Some decks (quite a few, really) have no
prayer of removing Sense Dep other than finding a way to get that
player ousted - which is largely not the best strategy when your
predator has played it on you.

It's not always crippling or insurmountable (if I'm playing
interchangable midcaps, or lots of untaps, etc, it just slows me down
a bit, for instance.) But it's a lot more likely to be a continuing,
unendable source of anti-fun than other similar cards, once it starts
being a problem.

If there was a more direct way to remove it - even one that is
relatively hard, but doesn't mandate what you must have in your
library - it'd be less of a problem and less actively-un-fun to see in
play.

win, I don't see it play a Sens Dep. And the majority of the time
that I see a Ravnos deck play a Sens Dep, it doesn't win. Which isn't
to say that it's a terrible card - it's a very strong card, but it
just seems like more than helping the player who uses it to win, it
just causes one player to lose/be pissed off. If it's his predator,

have to sit around doing nothing until the Ravnos player gets ousted.

burned. Heck, it could be worded exactly the same as Pentex

act to remove it.

> > that you can't always get every card that is very useful and goes in a
> > lot of decks, without the singles market, then you are bound to be
> > disappointed in life.
>
> Except there's nothing intrinsic to the game itself that forces the
> game to work that way, only the availability of cards.  Deflection
> only becomes expensive and rare on the singles market if it goes out
> of print.  If it stays in print, the problem is avoided.

The CCG sales model is based on the concept of cards of scarcity both
because there's a gambling aspect to opening packs and becaue it
encourages people to buy more cards when they can't have everything
easily. What does this have to do with the singles market? More than
is obvious. Perception of value helps marketing. CCG companies love
it when there are vibrant singles markets; it's better than the
alternative.

Anyway, this doesn't seem relevant to Deflection, which seems an
unlikely choice for keeping scarce, unlike, say, Shroud of Absence.
Can take comments at face value and believe that Deflection not being
reprinted was an unfortunate consequence of behind the scenes industry
stuff. That actually happens far more often than people realize,
especially with card art.

BTW, indications are, with some obvious exceptions, that CCGs are
dying out. Whether this is a lull in the short history of CCGs or a
permanent shaking out of the market is the question. Either way, the
newer model for card games is to sell fixed sets with all of the cards
for that set and to expand with more fixed sets.

> V:tES is not like M:tG, where you have rare cards that are completely
> superior to common cards, i.e. regular lands vs. dual lands.  In
> V:tES, the most powerful and useful cards are common and uncommon,
> which makes the game much better.  This allows new players to have an
> easier time getting into the game because they don't need to buy X
> copies of some powerful rare card to make a competitive deck.  Any
> trend which moves toward the increasing need for rare and/or out of
> print cards is a bad one and to be avoided.

There are a number of rare cards in V:TES that enable tournament level
decks that have no close substitutes. Also, if you want to give a CCG
grief, give it to the old Dragonball Z CCG where an ultrarare and a
common did exactly the same thing and the common got banned.

"Need" - what does need mean? Do I need Dreams of the Sphinx? The
Unmasking? Sudario Refraction? Palla Grande/Week of Nightmares? The
Erciyes Fragments? Anthelios? Villein?

No. But, then, you can play competitive Magic without any rares,
too. The difference is that with Magic you will have hardly any
choices whereas with V:TES you will have lots of choices (almost all
of which will be better with Dreams).

The reality is that CCG companies are trying to maximize profits and
the CCG model has been based on the idea of chase cards, including
chase staples. Every indication, from people deciding to play the
original Star Wars CCG even though mains were ultrarare to Magic
adding ultrarares in the last year, is that producing scarcity of
useful cards increases profits. It's interesting that more effort
isn't put into keeping certain cards unavailable. My unopened Third
Edition boxes, which were horribly devalued from the get go by the
production problems with the set, have been significantly devalued by
having Heart of Nizchetus, On the Qui Vive, et al getting reprinted.

Is scarcity pro-player? Of course not. We want to spend as little as
possible in our goals. Though, quite a few of us also like chase
cards for the challenge of collecting and to be able to look down upon
those poor saps who don't put a dozen Mythic Forms in all of their
decks. So, it's not cut and dried just as nothing in CCGs is ever cut
and dried.

I've frequently argued that CCGs scare off potential players when they
force them to invest heavily just to compete. So, yes, I can see
where not having a kajillion Deflections at hand is irksome. But,
then, I don't see a lot of people getting into V:TES while I hear of
plenty of collections full of commons being up for sale. And, just
think, trading for Deflection should be simplicity itself since the
card is almost valueless to people like me.

letting them be scarce for a year or so and then reprinting them in a
starter? Heart of Nizchetus is a paragon, I think, of V:TES' scarcity
model, where LSJ prints a shotgun blast of new stuff, some of it's
pretty good, and whatever seems to be the best (or players complain
about needing more of the most) gets reprinted in the next two sets.
Which works for me, if it means good cards provide a boost for the
singles market for this set, and then a boost again for the next one.

> "Need" - what does need mean?  Do I need Dreams of the Sphinx?

Well, frankly, I think if you want to be competitive, you do. But
luckily, all the cards in your (now truncated) list which I believe
both competitive AND casual players would want, have made it into
multiple sets and usually a starter. Dreams made it into 3 starters,

> of which will be better with Dreams).

gain pool. IMO, if we continue getting more of these things, and then
we get more reasonable ways to increase transfers, then Dreams will be
merely an option instead of a competitive necessity.

> The reality is that CCG companies are trying to maximize profits

The following stand, more or less:
More profits = less overhead + more boxes sold.

How do you sell more boxes? Well, you need to attract more players
(who then buy cards.)

But, the boxes alone cannot support the players. A healthy singles
market must support them.

Therefore, the game must be cheap enough to get in and play, by way of
cheap and plentiful good cards (which build a player base), but also
enough cards with good resale value that the secondary market can
thrive and support those players.

> Every indication...is that producing scarcity of
> useful cards increases profits.

No, not one indication, which is retaining players.

Wizards of the Coast declared recently that future Magic sets would
have fewer cards than past sets because players asked for it
repeatedly, and they believe it's increasingly wise to cater to the
players as the US/global economy weakens.

The "Mythic Rare" rarity was introduced at the same time, not only
because it drives little kids crazy to open a huge dragon that's a
"Mythic Rare", but also because it helps the secondary market. The MR
rarity is now about as rare as regular rares were before.

> isn't put into keeping certain cards unavailable.  My unopened Third
> Edition boxes, which were horribly devalued from the get go by the
> production problems with the set, have been significantly devalued by
> having Heart of Nizchetus, On the Qui Vive, et al getting reprinted.

This is the downside of speculation. Speculators are not guaranteed a
return on their investment, especially in an economic downturn, and
especially in a game where the designer has a history of reprinting
hard-to-find and oft-demanded cards, and the designer/company has
stated a preference to recruit new players and to be player-friendly.

I do see a lot of people getting into V:TES. Outside of searching
eBay, I don't know of any collections for sale.

Anyway, share your experiences, OK? I will read it!

following set since people won't know the sucktactitude of a set until
it's already sold (lots of set sales come early in the set's life).

downturn in economy, industry trend, whatever. I occasionally wonder

in an industry that doesn't do recalls and having the people who
normally express interest in sharing orders lacking an interest in
taking as much as normal, which was then followed by a lack of
artificially propping up the value of the set by avoiding certain
reprints until more inventory could be cleared.

My experiences? My experience is that while people still play that we
used to have 3-4 storyline events and now struggle to have 2, that we
used to have 3-4 meaningful standard constructed tournaments a year
and now we only have them when Ira comes up with a qualifier weekend,
that when I used to go to Northern Virginia, a double digit turnout at
someone's house was possible where now I might comprise 20% of the
tournament turnout, that I used to keep up with at least 3 CCGs and
now wish I had more money to travel to play one meaningfully, that the
rare times I have read Kravdraa, I wasn't seeing this healthy Seattle
environment you were talking about (I guess things have improved this
year), that once upon a time we had a 22 player turnout at a local
convention (with a 17 player, losers game) and had the number of
pickup tables go down to one around 2 or 3AM where now I'm amazed that

were L5R Kotei at local cons, that the Shadowfist crowd used to show
up to one of the cons, that people did crazy stuff like run demos for
niche CCGs.

But, then, I'm not nearly as plugged into the industry as I once was,
so I don't put tremendous weight on my experiences. I seem to get
into niche CCGs that require tremendous amounts of work on volunteers'
parts to even maintain groups. Magic and other major CCGs moved out
of local cons for good reasons. We'd have more tournaments if we
didn't bother asking the players whether they wanted to have them and

better? Why aren't there rarity indicators on cards? Why can't
people come up with better prize ideas than unique promos? Why don't
storyline events rock the world and make for significant changes in
the game in future sets? Why isn't Dominate banned?

The structure of Sets (Big Core Set with lots of staple cards and a
handy smattering of new shiney stuff + 2 or 3 baby sets of random
stuff) is something that probably doesn't need to be changed too
much. Every two or three years a glut of "staple cards" whacks into
the market and people's collections before being tapered out over the
next 3 smaller sets (like KMW, Legacies of Blood, Sword of Caine,
Twilight Rebellion...). It seems to work for WW and it's not too
bad. Sure I'd be more tempted to buy more over a longer period of
time (say if there was a 9 month delay between sets rather than 6
months) but *shrug* I doubt my quiet voice in the gale will change
that tactic.

Sure, the way to keep any community vibrant is to regularly and
frequently meet with "same but different" experiences. Works for the
Charismatic Church in the US, works for D&D gamers (to an extent)...
should work for a CCG. The Storyline concept (and BYO Storyline)
would appear to be a unique thing to V:TES probably because it stemmed
from an RPG originally. Personally, I want to do more and see more
Storyline impact in the cards. I don't know how much it takes, but
I'm guessing that Fee Stake: Perth (which is a city from my lovely
homeland) came about because of a BYO Storyline... and I like that
fact. I think people around the world would be interested in seeing
more V:TES cards connected to where they live. It's a tactic that
plays to sentimentality and pride in "your place".

There are a lot of things VTES does better than MtG in my opinion.
While there are more things they could be doing... let's make sure we
don't kill the patient to cure the disease. I'll take a "slightly
sick VTES" over a "Zombie Corpse MtG-Clone".
